transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2027-11-18 16:00 PT
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Silva (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NimbleHealth Eng Mgr), Jon Redding (NimbleHealth SRE), Liam O'Connor (NimbleHealth Product)

Summary (auto): triage of timeouts/5xx during last week's pilot surge; plan for load test and retry tuning

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um let's get started. I know last week you saw a pretty sharp spike in timeouts and some 5xxs, so want to run through what we found and next steps. Marcus, do you want to start with the quick findings?
[00:18] Marcus: Yeah, sure. Quick tl;dr — we saw two main patterns. One was client visible timeouts at around 1.2% of requests during the 03:00 UTC surge window, the other was transient 5xxs that look correlated with high batch sizes and a small set of model-serving nodes that were cold on KV cache. So basically some requests hit a node that didn't have warmed KV and incurred extra latency, pushing them past client timeouts.
[00:45] Priya: Just to clarify, when you say "KV cash" — you mean the key-value cache for decoder state, right? We saw the logs, but some of the names were, um, truncated so it's hard to map.
[00:58] Marcus: Yeah, KV cache, sorry the auto transcript sometimes— it's KV cache for the attention cache. On about 0.3% of tokens we saw a cold miss and that pushed a handful of requests over the 5s client threshold.
[01:14] Jon: And the 5xxs, were they coming back as 502 or 5xx internal? I think we had a handful of 502s and some 504s from our gateway.
[01:22] Marcus: Mostly 502-ish gateway errors, with downstream timeouts cascading. There's also a rate-limit throttling pattern so some requests retried immediately and created short retry storms.
[01:34] Liam: So is this mostly an artifact of large batch sizes you recommended earlier? We had batch size bumped to 16 to get throughput lower cost, do we need to back that off?
[01:43] Avery: Good question. This is the classic latency vs cost tradeoff. Marcus, can you explain how batch size interacts here?
[01:50] Marcus: Sure. At high concurrency, large batch sizes increase tail latency variance. If a node has to do the extra fetch for KV cache warmup, that request becomes a long tail and can get dropped by client if their timeout is tight. Also if multiple clients backoff badly, retries can increase effective qps and push other nodes into higher batch sizes, it's a feedback loop.
[02:14] Priya: We run an internal client timeout at 5 seconds — that's non-negotiable for our UX, breaking the flow hurts conversions.
[02:21] Avery: Understood. So we should look at changing server-side behavior: smaller max batch size for this workload, tighten our retry budget and add jitter, and enable aggressive KV-cache prewarm on the hot path.
[02:34] Jon: Prewarm — is that something Redwood can do automatically or do we need to trigger synthetic requests from our side?
[02:40] Marcus: We have two levers. One is server-side background warmers which we can enable for the pilot (costs extra cycles), the other is a suggested probe policy from the client to warm small prefixes before user requests (cheap on client side). We'll trial server warmers for the next flood test.
[02:58] Liam: How about rate limits — we noticed 429 spikes before the 502s. Can we do windowing or burst allowance changes?
[03:06] Marcus: The platform supports token-bucket style limits and per-tenant sliding windows. For the pilot we can increase the short-term burst allowance and add queuing upstream so spikes smooth out. But that increases short-term cost.
[03:20] Priya: Cost is a concern, but availability is higher priority during the pilot. We're open to a temporary increase if it keeps the UX intact while we iterate.
[03:28] Avery: Cool. Let's talk concrete experiment plan. We'll run a controlled flood with new config: reduce max batch to 8, enable server-side KV prewarm, increase short-burst allowance by 30%, and set a conservative retry budget with exponential backoff and jitter. Marcus, can you run that?
[03:46] Marcus: Yep. I'm thinking we do a 2-hour run with ramp-up to 1k qps then steady for 60 minutes and ramp down. I'll record detailed traces and token-level latency histograms.
[03:57] Jon: Please include the ingress gateway logs and our APM traces — the correlation is what matters.
[04:03] Marcus: Yep, include both. Also I'll instrument to log which node served each request so we can spot the cold nodes.
[04:11] Priya: On the logs, we found one conf diff that might be related — our autoscaler had more aggressive downscaling at night which may have left cold pools. I'm pulling the diff and will share.
[04:21] Avery: Great. Quick aside — security/compliance question: Priya asked earlier about audit logs and KMS for Private deployment options. Is that still on the table for this pilot?
[04:31] Priya: Not necessarily for the pilot, but if we go to Dedicated or Private we need KMS integration and SOC2 evidence. We wanted to confirm Redwood provides those when we move off-hosted.
[04:41] Avery: Yes, we have a Private deployment option with customer-managed KMS and SOC2 artifacts. I'll send the security pack after the call.
[04:49] Liam: Back to retries — one pattern we saw was aggressive client retries with no jitter, that caused a retry storm. Can Redwood inject a retry-after or is that purely client-side?
[04:59] Marcus: There's an HTTP throttling header we can emit and clients can respect. We can also implement server-side rate limiting with coordinated retry-after semantics. But best practice is client backoff with jitter; we'll share a sample client spec.
[05:12] Priya: We'll update our client library quickly. Jon can you own that?
[05:16] Jon: Yep can do. I'll instrument and push a small change to add randomized exponential backoff.
[05:20] Avery: Awesome. Any other anomalies from the logs you want to surface?
[05:24] Priya: One weird thing — a subset of requests were routed to a legacy model variant with larger memory footprint; that variant had slightly different kernel behavior and higher latency. Not sure why routing chose it for a few tenants.
[05:36] Marcus: That sounds like a routing policy drift — possibly a model homing fallback when capacity tightness happened. I'll dig into routing logs to see why those variants were selected.
[05:44] Liam: If that's the case, can we pin a variant for our pilot tenant so it never falls back to the legacy model?
[05:50] Avery: Yes, we can pin model version for your tenant. That avoids those surprises.
[05:54] Priya: Good, please do that.
[05:56] Marcus: I'll set a tenant pin for NimbleHealth to the verified low-latency variant for the flood run.
[06:02] Avery: Recap — Marcus runs flood test with reduced batch and server warmers; Priya shares traces and config diff; Jon adds jittered backoff in client lib; Avery sends pricing and security pack. We'll reconvene next week to review results.
[06:15] Liam: One last Q — what's our threshold to shift to Dedicated for production?
[06:20] Avery: We usually consider Dedicated when sustained p95 is above your SLA or when tenant isolation is required. We'll show you numbers from the flood and propose a cost/latency breakpoint.
[06:31] Jon: Ok that helps. Thanks everyone.
[06:33] Avery: Thanks — we'll follow up with notes and action items.

--- End transcript ---
questions: Q: Can Redwood enable server-side KV prewarm? A: Yes, can enable for pilot (cost tradeoff)
Q: Can we pin model variant to avoid legacy fallbacks? A: Yes, Redwood will pin tenant to low-latency variant for the run
